```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(SMSD)
fixed <- function(x, digits) formatC(x, digits = digits, format = "f")
```

## The Research Question

A large organization trains new employees face to face at a central
site. Two cheaper formats are proposed: one-on-one video calls, and a
hybrid of recorded material followed by a shorter call. Face to face
training costs far more per trainee than either alternative, because of
travel and lodging. The organization will spend a fixed amount on a study
and wants to know whether the average of the two alternatives is no
worse than the face to face format by more than a margin that matters,
or is equivalent to it within such a margin. This is the application
that motivates Chattopadhyay, Bandyopadhyay, Kelley, and Padalunkal
(2025), and the same structure arises whenever several groups with
unequal sampling costs are compared under a fixed budget: multisite
program evaluations in education, marketing experiments across regions,
surveys that compare strata.

With μ<sub>1</sub> the mean score after face to face training and
μ<sub>2</sub> and μ<sub>3</sub> the means after the two alternatives, the
quantity of interest is the contrast (Equation 1 of the article)

<p style="text-align: center;">&psi; = &minus;&mu;<sub>1</sub> + &frac12; &mu;<sub>2</sub> + &frac12; &mu;<sub>3</sub></p>

How should the budget be divided among the three groups so that ψ is
estimated as precisely as possible? The answer depends on the population
variances, which are unknown before the study. A fixed sample size plan
has to take them from a guess or from a separate pilot study (the
approach of Luh & Guo, 2016). The sequential procedure learns them from
the data as the data arrive, in the purely sequential tradition surveyed
by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009), and it counts the pilot observations
against the same budget and uses them in the analysis.

## The Method

Take a contrast ψ of *K* population means with weights
*c*<sub>*i*</sub>, the sum over the populations of *c*<sub>*i*</sub>
μ<sub>*i*</sub>. Its estimate is the same weighted sum of the sample
means, and the variance of the estimate is the sum of
*c*<sub>*i*</sub><sup>2</sup> σ<sub>*i*</sub><sup>2</sup> /
*n*<sub>*i*</sub>, where σ<sub>*i*</sub> is the standard deviation of
population *i* and *n*<sub>*i*</sub> its sample size. An observation from
population *i* costs *a*<sub>*i*</sub>, and the total budget is
*A*<sub>0</sub>. Theorem 1 of the article gives the sample sizes that
minimize the variance when the total cost, the sum of *a*<sub>*i*</sub>
*n*<sub>*i*</sub>, equals the budget (its Equation 12),

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>n</i><sub><i>i</i>0</sub> = <i>A</i><sub>0</sub> |<i>c</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>| &sigma;<sub><i>i</i></sub> / (&radic;<i>a</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> &times; &Sigma;<sub><i>l</i></sub> |<i>c</i><sub><i>l</i></sub>| &sigma;<sub><i>l</i></sub> &radic;<i>a</i><sub><i>l</i></sub>)</p>

and the minimized variance (Equation 13),

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>V</i><sub><i>o</i></sub> = (&Sigma;<sub><i>i</i></sub> |<i>c</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>| &sigma;<sub><i>i</i></sub> &radic;<i>a</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>)<sup>2</sup> / <i>A</i><sub>0</sub></p>

A group receives more observations when its scores vary more, when its
weight in the contrast is larger, and when it is cheaper to sample.
Minimizing the variance is what maximizes the power of the tests
described below.

Because the σ<sub>*i*</sub> are unknown, the sequential procedure
replaces them with the current sample standard deviations
*s*<sub>*i*</sub>. Group *i* has met its criterion when its sample size
*N*<sub>*i*</sub> satisfies (Equation 18)

<p style="text-align: center;"><i>N</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> &ge; <i>A</i><sub>0</sub> |<i>c</i><sub><i>i</i></sub>| <i>s</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> / (&radic;<i>a</i><sub><i>i</i></sub> &times; &Sigma;<sub><i>l</i></sub> |<i>c</i><sub><i>l</i></sub>| <i>s</i><sub><i>l</i></sub> &radic;<i>a</i><sub><i>l</i></sub>)</p>

and sampling ends when every group has met its criterion or when the
budget cannot pay for another needed observation. The functions divide
the work as follows.

| Step | Function |
|---|---|
| Plan with assumed standard deviations | `seq_budget_optimal()` |
| Choose the pilot size | `seq_budget_pilot()` |
| Check the data in hand | `seq_budget()` |
| Choose the group for the next observation | `seq_budget_next()` |
| Decide noninferiority, superiority, inferiority, or equivalence | `decide_seq_budget_*()` |
| Study the design by simulation before collecting data | `seq_budget_sensitivity()` |

## A Priori Planning

The article's own illustration (p. 430) has three groups, a cost of 30
per observation in each, and a budget of 10,000. When the products of
weight and standard deviation, |*c*<sub>*i*</sub>| σ<sub>*i*</sub>, are
equal, the optimal size is the same in every group:

```{r plan-equal}
plan <- seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = c(-1, 0.5, 0.5),
  sigmas           = c(1, 2, 2),
  cost_per_group   = c(30, 30, 30),
  budget           = 10000
)
plan$n_per_group
plan$minimum_variance
```

The sizes are not whole numbers, and they cannot simply be rounded up:
112 per group would cost `r format(3 * 30 * 112, big.mark = ",")`. The
article rounds to 111 per group, 333 observations in all, at a cost of
`r format(3 * 30 * 111, big.mark = ",")`. A few units of the budget go
unspent whenever the unit costs do not divide what is left, and this is
how the sequential procedure ends as well.

Costs are rarely equal. Suppose face to face training costs 500 per
trainee (the figure the article uses), a video call 150, and the hybrid
format 250, with a budget of 50,000 (again the article's figure) and
scores on a 30 point assessment whose standard deviations are thought to
be about 3, 3.5, and 2.5:

```{r plan-unequal}
weights <- c(-1, 0.5, 0.5)
costs   <- c(500, 150, 250)
budget  <- 50000

plan <- seq_budget_optimal(
  contrast_weights = weights,
  sigmas           = c(3, 3.5, 2.5),
  cost_per_group   = costs,
  budget           = budget
)
plan$n_per_group
sum(costs * plan$n_per_group)
sqrt(plan$minimum_variance)
```

The face to face group carries twice the weight of either alternative,
yet it does not receive twice the observations, because each of its
observations costs two to more than three times as much. The last line
is the smallest standard error of the contrast estimate that this budget
can buy if the assumed standard deviations are right.

## The Sequential Workflow

The standard deviations above were guesses. The sequential procedure
does not need them. It starts with a pilot from every group, which is
paid for from the same budget. The article requires at least two
observations per group and advises more, because variance estimates from
very small samples are unstable (p. 431); its simulations used 10.

```{r pilot}
m_0 <- seq_budget_pilot(m_0 = 10)
m_0 * sum(costs)
```

The pilot costs `r format(m_0 * sum(costs), big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(budget, big.mark = ",")`. To have data to work with, the
scores are simulated here from populations whose true contrast is zero
(the alternatives are exactly as effective as face to face training on
average); in a study each new score would come from the next trainee.

```{r seq-first-check}
set.seed(113)
true_means <- c(15, 15, 15)
true_sds   <- c(3, 3.5, 2.5)
new_score  <- function(g, k = 1) rnorm(k, true_means[g], true_sds[g])

scores <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)

out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
out
attr(out, "n_per_group")
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
seq_budget_next(out)
```

The weights and costs are matched to the groups by position. If they are
named and the list of groups is named too, the names must agree in
order; `seq_budget()` stops otherwise, so that, for example, weights
typed in the order of the design are not applied to a list that
`split()` has put in alphabetical order.

After the pilot every group is below its criterion, so sampling
continues. `seq_budget_next()` names the group that should receive the
next observation: by default the one furthest below its estimated
optimal size, among the groups whose next observation the remaining
budget can pay for. Because it never names a group that cannot be paid
for, a study that follows it one observation at a time cannot overspend.
The whole study is then a short loop (the helper `term()` pulls one row
out of a check, here to record the running cost):

```{r seq-loop}
term <- function(check, name) check$value[check$term == name]

cost_path <- term(out, "current_total_cost")
repeat {
  out <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores[[g]] <- c(scores[[g]], new_score(g))
  cost_path <- c(cost_path, term(out, "current_total_cost") + costs[g])
}
out
```

```{r seq-loop-summary}
attr(out, "n_per_group")
attr(out, "criterion_per_group")
max(cost_path) <= budget
```

```{r cost-path, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.6, fig.alt = "Running total cost of the study against the number of observations added after the pilot, rising in steps to the budget line without crossing it."}
plot(seq_along(cost_path) - 1, cost_path, type = "s",
     xlab = "Observations added after the pilot",
     ylab = "Total cost so far", ylim = c(0, budget))
abline(h = budget, lty = 2)
```

### Why Sampling Ends With Sizes Below the Criteria

Sampling has ended (`is_satisfied` is `TRUE`) although the current total
sample size (`r attr(out, "current_n")`) is below the total of the criteria
(`r attr(out, "criterion_n")`). The note under the printed check gives the
reason: sampling ended because the budget could not pay for another
observation that was still needed, not because every group reached its
criterion.
The attributes separate the two ways of ending:

```{r why-stopped}
attr(out, "rule_met")
attr(out, "budget_exhausted")
attr(out, "is_satisfied")
attr(out, "remaining_budget")
```

`rule_met` is `TRUE` when every group has met its criterion.
`budget_exhausted` is `TRUE` when at least one group is still below its
criterion and what is left of the budget cannot pay for one more
observation from any such group. `seq_budget_next()` returns `NA`
exactly when one of the two holds, and `is_satisfied` is `TRUE` then
too, with one exception that is taken up below: a study in which the
variance of some group is unusable is never reported as satisfied.
`seq_report()` words the result for a methods section and names the
ending for what it is:

```{r report}
seq_report(out)
```

Ending by the budget is the normal case, not a failure. Multiply each
right hand side of Equation 18 by its unit cost and add them up: the sum
is *A*<sub>0</sub>, whatever the standard deviations are. Judged on the
current data, therefore, every group can be at or above its criterion
without passing the budget only when each sample size equals its target
exactly, which requires every target to be a whole number. Otherwise the
procedure runs until what is left of the budget (here
`r attr(out, "remaining_budget")`) is less than the cost of any
observation still needed, just as 333 observations at 30 each leave 10 of
10,000 unspent in the article's illustration.

```{r short-groups, include = FALSE}
short <- which(!attr(out, "met_per_group"))
short_txt <- if (length(short) == 1L) {
  paste("group", short, "was")
} else {
  paste("groups", paste(short, collapse = " and "), "were")
}
```

Only the groups that still need observations count. At the end of this
run `r short_txt` still below the criterion, and a cheaper group that had
already met its criterion would not have kept the study going.
Conversely, when the most expensive group can no longer be paid for but a
cheaper one still needs observations, the study continues with the
cheaper one.

If the data handed to `seq_budget()` already cost more than the budget
(a pilot the budget cannot pay for, or a loop that added observations
without asking `seq_budget_next()`), the check says so in a note and
sets the attribute `budget_exceeded`:

```{r exceeded}
over <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = 40000)
attr(over, "budget_exceeded")
writeLines(strwrap(attr(over, "notes"), width = 72))
```

### When Observations Arrive in Batches

`seq_budget_next()` names one group for one observation. A study that
collects several observations at a time takes them from the group it
names, but no more than the remaining budget pays for and no more than
the group is still short of its criterion, and then checks again. The
loop below does that for batches of up to 10, starting from the same
pilot scores as the loop above.

```{r batch-loop}
batch <- 10

set.seed(113)
batched <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)
repeat {
  out_b <- seq_budget(batched, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                      budget = budget)
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_b)
  if (is.na(g)) break
  affordable <- floor(attr(out_b, "remaining_budget") / costs[g])
  short <- ceiling(attr(out_b, "criterion_per_group")[g] -
                     attr(out_b, "n_per_group")[g])
  batched[[g]] <- c(batched[[g]],
                    new_score(g, min(batch, affordable, max(1, short))))
}
attr(out_b, "n_per_group")
term(out_b, "current_total_cost")
attr(out_b, "budget_exceeded")
```

The study ends within the budget, with
`r paste(attr(out_b, "n_per_group"), collapse = ", ")` observations in
the three groups where the loop that checked after every observation
ended with `r paste(attr(out, "n_per_group"), collapse = ", ")`. A loop
that adds a whole batch whatever the remaining budget is can overspend;
the check then sets `budget_exceeded`, as in the example above, and the
budget constraint no longer holds for its result.

### When a Group Shows No Variation

With a small pilot and coarsely scored data, every observation in a
group can be the same. Its sample variance is then zero, Equation 18
gives it a target of zero, and the stopping rule as printed in the
article would end the sampling from that group with a variance estimate
of zero. A variance of zero is not an estimate, and `seq_budget()`
treats it as every check in the package treats an unusable variance,
which is a deliberate departure from the article: the rule is reported
as not met, the attribute `variance_unusable` is `TRUE`, and the printed
notes say so. (The same holds when the scores of a group agree to about
ten significant digits, so that whatever variance is computed is
rounding error.)

```{r constant-group}
ratings <- list(c(4, 4, 4), c(3, 5, 4), c(2, 4, 5))
flat <- seq_budget(ratings, weights, cost_per_group = costs, budget = budget)
flat
attr(flat, "variance_unusable")
seq_budget_next(flat)
```

`seq_budget_next()` names such a group whenever no group whose variance
can be used has fewer observations than it has, so the group is
sampled at the pace of the least sampled of the others until its scores
differ; one or two more observations usually settle it. A group that
really is constant (a ceiling or a floor on the measure) keeps that pace
to the end, which can take a large part of the budget when the group is
expensive, and the study ends with `is_satisfied` still `FALSE` and a
result that the decision functions refuse. If a group shows no variation
after more than a few observations beyond the pilot, stop and reconsider
the measure before spending the rest of the budget.

## Hypothesis Decisions

When sampling has ended, the estimate and its standard error are used
for the test the study was designed for. The four decision functions are
one family. Each is a one-sided test at level `alpha_level`, 0.05 by
default as in the article's tables, computed from the contrast estimate
and its standard error, the square root of the row `variance`;
equivalence is two such tests. None of them reads the interval printed on
the check, whose confidence level is two-sided, so the confidence level
of the check does not enter a decision. Below, SE stands for that
standard error and *z*<sub>α</sub> for the upper 100α percent point of the
standard normal distribution (1.645 for α = 0.05).

The article formulates noninferiority with inferiority as the null
hypothesis (its Equations 6 and 7): for a margin δ > 0 fixed in advance
(the article's |ψ<sub>0</sub>|), the null hypothesis is ψ ≤ −δ and the
alternative is ψ > −δ. The null hypothesis is rejected at one-sided level
α when the estimate is above −δ + *z*<sub>α</sub> SE (Equation C3). The
formulation assumes that a larger response is better, which is why the
contrast was written with the face to face format entering negatively.
The `margin` argument is the size of the margin, a positive number. The
article illustrates equivalence with a margin of 1.25 points; the same
margin is used here.

```{r noninferiority}
decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 1.25)
```

```{r noninferiority-values, include = FALSE}
ni <- decide_seq_budget_noninferiority(out, margin = 1.25)
est <- term(out, "contrast")
se <- sqrt(term(out, "variance"))
lower_90 <- est - qnorm(0.95) * se
upper_90 <- est + qnorm(0.95) * se
```

The estimate is `r fixed(est, 2)` with a standard error of
`r fixed(se, 2)`, so the estimate minus 1.645 standard errors, the lower
limit of a 90 percent interval, is `r fixed(lower_90, 2)`, which is
`r if (ni) "above" else "not above"` −1.25: inferiority is
`r if (ni) "rejected, and noninferiority is declared" else "not rejected"`.
`r if (!ni) "Failing to reject is not evidence of inferiority."`

Equivalence is two one-sided tests, each at level α (Equations 11 and
C15): the contrast is declared to lie between the margins ψ<sub>1</sub>
and ψ<sub>2</sub> when the estimate is above ψ<sub>1</sub> +
*z*<sub>α</sub> SE and below ψ<sub>2</sub> − *z*<sub>α</sub> SE. The two
margins are given as they are, with their signs.

```{r equivalence}
decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -1.25, margin_upper = 1.25)
```

```{r equivalence-values, include = FALSE}
eq <- decide_seq_budget_equivalence(out, margin_lower = -1.25,
                                    margin_upper = 1.25)
width_90 <- upper_90 - lower_90
se_from_zero <- abs(est) / se
direction <- if (est > 0) "above" else "below"
eq_txt <- if (eq) {
  paste("Both limits lie inside the margins, so the formats are declared",
        "equivalent within 1.25 points.")
} else {
  paste0(
    if (upper_90 >= 1.25) "Its upper limit is above 1.25"
    else "Its lower limit is below −1.25",
    ", so equivalence within 1.25 points is not declared. ",
    if (width_90 < 2.5) paste0(
      "The interval is not too wide for the margins: it is ",
      fixed(width_90, 2), " wide, and the band between them is 2.5 wide. ",
      "It crosses a margin because the estimate in this run lies ",
      fixed(se_from_zero, 1), " standard errors ", direction,
      " the true contrast of zero. The scores were simulated from formats ",
      "that are equally effective, so the failure to declare equivalence ",
      "is a Type II error of this run and not a verdict on the budget."
    ) else paste(
      "The interval is wider than the band between the margins, which is",
      "2.5 wide, so no estimate could have led to a declaration."
    )
  )
}
```

The 90 percent interval runs from `r fixed(lower_90, 2)` to
`r fixed(upper_90, 2)`. `r eq_txt`

How often a study on this budget declares equivalence when the formats
are equally effective can be worked out before any data are collected.
The test declares it when the estimate is within 1.25 − *z*<sub>α</sub>
SE of zero. Take for SE the smallest standard error this budget allows,
from the plan in the section on a priori planning, and take the estimate
to be normally distributed around a true contrast of zero:

```{r equivalence-power}
se_best <- sqrt(plan$minimum_variance)    # smallest standard error
reach <- 1.25 - qnorm(0.95) * se_best     # declared when |estimate| < reach
c(reach = reach,
  noninferiority = pnorm(reach / se_best),
  equivalence = 2 * pnorm(reach / se_best) - 1)
```

By this approximation the budget declares noninferiority in about
`r fixed(100 * pnorm(reach / se_best), 0)` percent of studies and
equivalence in about `r fixed(100 * (2 * pnorm(reach / se_best) - 1), 0)`
percent when the true contrast is zero. Equivalence asks more of a study
than noninferiority does, because the estimate has to stay clear of both
margins.

The other two functions are the one-sided tests against a single margin,
which is given with its sign. For a margin *m*,
`decide_seq_budget_superiority()` tests the null hypothesis ψ ≤ *m*
against the alternative ψ > *m*. With a positive margin it is the
article's superiority test (Equations 8 and 9), with a margin of zero it
asks whether the alternatives are better than face to face training at
all, and noninferiority is its special case `margin = -abs(delta)`:

```{r superiority}
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -abs(1.25))
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0)
```

```{r superiority-values, include = FALSE}
sup_0 <- decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0)
sup_0_strict <- decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0,
                                              alpha_level = 0.025)
```

The first line repeats the noninferiority decision, because a contrast
above −δ and noninferiority with margin δ are the same hypothesis.
`r if (sup_0) paste0("The second declares the alternatives better than face to face training, because the lower limit of the 90 percent interval (", fixed(lower_90, 2), ") is just above zero. These scores were simulated with a true contrast of zero, so this is a Type I error, which a test at level 0.05 makes in about one study in twenty when the true contrast equals the margin.", if (!eq) " It has the same cause as the failure to declare equivalence: one estimate that came out well above the true value." else "") else "The second does not declare the alternatives better than face to face training, as it should not: these scores were simulated with a true contrast of zero."`
`decide_seq_budget_inferiority()` is the mirror image, the null
hypothesis ψ ≥ *m* against the alternative ψ < *m*: it concludes that the
contrast is below the margin, with that conclusion as the alternative
hypothesis. It is not the article's noninferiority test, in which
inferiority is the null hypothesis.

```{r inferiority}
decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 0)
```

These two tests are the halves of the equivalence test. In the article
they are its Equations C11 to C14: equivalence between ψ<sub>1</sub> and
ψ<sub>2</sub> is declared exactly when the superiority test at
ψ<sub>1</sub> and the inferiority test at ψ<sub>2</sub> both reject.

```{r two-halves}
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = -1.25) &&
  decide_seq_budget_inferiority(out, margin = 1.25)
```

A stricter test is a smaller `alpha_level`. The limits that a test at
level α compares with its margins are those of a check computed with
`conf_level = 1 - 2 * alpha_level`; for the default level that is the 90
percent interval quoted above.

```{r levels}
decide_seq_budget_superiority(out, margin = 0, alpha_level = 0.025)

out_90 <- seq_budget(scores, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                     budget = budget, conf_level = 1 - 2 * 0.05)
c(term(out_90, "lower_limit"), term(out_90, "upper_limit"))
```

At one-sided level 0.025 the alternatives are
`r if (sup_0_strict) "still" else "no longer"` declared better than face
to face training.

The level of each test is stated for one decision, made when sampling
has ended. Asked for a decision earlier, the functions return it with a
warning that it is provisional.

## What to Expect Before the Study

`seq_budget_sensitivity()` runs the whole procedure many times for
assumed means, standard deviations, costs, and budget, and reports what
it delivers. Here the alternatives are taken to be exactly as effective
as face to face training, so the rejection rate of the noninferiority
test is its power at a true contrast of zero.

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means       = true_means,
  true_sds         = true_sds,
  contrast_weights = weights,
  cost_per_group   = costs,
  budget           = budget,
  margin           = 1.25,
  G                = 400,
  seed             = 113,
  m_0              = 10
)
print(sens, digits = 4)
```

No replication went over the budget (`pct_within_budget` is
`r term(sens, "pct_within_budget")`), which holds by construction. The
mean final sizes are close to the optimal ones. Three rows describe the
variance of the estimator and are to be read against
`optimal_variance`, the smallest the budget allows
(`r fixed(term(sens, "optimal_variance"), 3)`): the mean of the estimated
variance at stopping (`r fixed(term(sens, "mean_estimated_variance"), 3)`),
the mean true variance at the final sample sizes
(`r fixed(term(sens, "mean_true_variance"), 3)`, which no allocation
within the budget can push below the optimum), and the variance actually
observed over the replications
(`r fixed(term(sens, "empirical_variance"), 3)`, the noisiest of the
three). The interval covered the true contrast in
`r fixed(100 * term(sens, "coverage"), 1)` percent of the
`r term(sens, "replications")` replications (Monte Carlo standard error
`r fixed(100 * sqrt(term(sens, "coverage") * (1 - term(sens, "coverage")) / term(sens, "replications")), 1)`
percentage points), and with a margin of 1.25 this budget rejects
inferiority in about
`r fixed(100 * term(sens, "noninferiority_rejection_rate"), 1)` percent
of studies when the formats are in fact equally effective (Monte Carlo
standard error
`r fixed(100 * sqrt(term(sens, "noninferiority_rejection_rate") * (1 - term(sens, "noninferiority_rejection_rate")) / term(sens, "replications")), 1)`
percentage points), which agrees with the
`r fixed(100 * pnorm(reach / se_best), 0)` percent that the normal
approximation gave in the section on hypothesis decisions.

Two cautions. First, the interval and the tests are asymptotic. The
estimated variance tends to run slightly below the true one (sample
standard deviations underestimate population ones on average, and the
allocation follows them). The Details of `?seq_budget_sensitivity`
report runs of 10,000 replications of five designs with a pilot of 10
and about 15 to 120 observations per group: coverage of the 95 percent
interval was 0.936 to 0.949 for normal populations and 0.925 to 0.941
for skewed ones, and the noninferiority test, with the true contrast
exactly at the margin and a nominal level of 0.05, rejected in 0.050 to
0.061 of studies for normal populations and in 0.040 to 0.085 for skewed
ones. A smaller pilot makes the shortfall larger, and the minimum pilot
of two makes it much larger; the help page of `seq_budget_pilot()` gives
measured figures, and the `m_0` argument of `seq_budget_sensitivity()`
shows the effect for a design of interest. Second, the procedure makes
the most of a budget; it does not promise a given power. A study that
needs more must raise the budget or accept a wider margin. (The values
above are shown to four significant digits; the stored values are not
rounded. A reported analysis deserves more replications than the
`r term(sens, "replications")` used to keep this vignette quick.)

## The Article's First Passage Rule

In the article a population stops being sampled the first time it meets
its criterion and is never sampled again, and the populations still open
receive one observation each per stage, in decreasing order of their
standard deviations (pp. 429 to 430). A check sees only the data in
hand, so by default `seq_budget()` judges every group afresh at each
check: a group that met its criterion earlier and has fallen below it
again, because the other standard deviations moved, receives further
observations, and the next observation always goes to the group furthest
below its estimated optimal size. That default is this package's
choice, not the article's procedure. For the article's first passage
rule, hand each check the groups that the previous check closed and ask
for the article's order:

```{r first-passage}
set.seed(113)
scores_fp <- lapply(1:3, new_score, k = m_0)
closed <- NULL
repeat {
  out_fp <- seq_budget(scores_fp, weights, cost_per_group = costs,
                       budget = budget, closed = closed)
  closed <- attr(out_fp, "met_per_group")
  g <- seq_budget_next(out_fp, order = "rounds")
  if (is.na(g)) break
  scores_fp[[g]] <- c(scores_fp[[g]], new_score(g))
}
attr(out_fp, "n_per_group")
attr(out_fp, "rule_met")
attr(out_fp, "remaining_budget")
```

Under this rule every group can have met its criterion, each at its own
time, with part of the budget still unspent. (The loop is the package's
reading of the article's sequence rather than a step for step copy:
`?seq_budget_next` lists three details that differ, the main one being
that a check judges every open group each time, where the article
judges a population only after an observation drawn from it.) The two
readings can be
compared for a design with the `procedure` argument of
`seq_budget_sensitivity()`:

```{r first-passage-sens}
sens_fp <- seq_budget_sensitivity(
  true_means, true_sds, weights, costs, budget,
  margin = 1.25, G = 400, seed = 113, m_0 = 10,
  procedure = "first_passage"
)
rows <- c("mean_total_cost", "pct_rule_met", "mean_n_1", "mean_n_2",
          "mean_n_3", "mean_true_variance", "coverage")
data.frame(
  term = rows,
  reallocate = round(sens$value[match(rows, sens$term)], 3),
  first_passage = round(sens_fp$value[match(rows, sens_fp$term)], 3)
)
```

Under the article's rule about
`r fixed(term(sens_fp, "pct_rule_met"), 0)` percent of the studies ended
with every group having met its criterion and money left over; under the
default
`r if (term(sens, "pct_rule_met") == 0) "none did" else paste(fixed(term(sens, "pct_rule_met"), 0), "percent did")`,
and on average
`r fixed(term(sens, "mean_total_cost") - term(sens_fp, "mean_total_cost"), 0)`
more of the budget was spent. The two readings give intervals of
practically the same quality. In the simulations reported in the Details
of `?seq_budget` (three designs from Table 1 of the article, each with a
budget of 5,000 and a pilot of 10, for normal and for skewed
populations), the default left about 10 to 12 of the budget unspent where
the first passage rule left 19 to 42, the true variance of the estimator
at the final sample sizes was 0.2 to 1.0 percent smaller under the
default, and coverage differed by at most 0.006, in either direction.
The difference in coverage in the table above
(`r fixed(term(sens, "coverage"), 3)` against
`r fixed(term(sens_fp, "coverage"), 3)`) is within Monte Carlo error at
`r term(sens, "replications")` replications, where each figure has a
standard error of about
`r fixed(sqrt(term(sens, "coverage") * (1 - term(sens, "coverage")) / term(sens, "replications")), 3)`.
